content: There is substantial evidence indicating significant health risks for both infants and mothers when breastfeeding is not practiced. In 2003, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of an infant's life, with continued breastfeeding as a key component of the infant's diet for at least two years. However, breastfeeding rates in many countries fall short of these recommendations. The objectives of this review were to: 1. Describe various types of breastfeeding support provided to healthy breastfeeding mothers with healthy term infants. 2. Evaluate the effectiveness of different breastfeeding support interventions, distinguishing between those offering only breastfeeding support and those combining breastfeeding support with broader maternal and child health interventions (referred to as breastfeeding plus support). 3. Assess the impact of specific intervention characteristics, including the type of support (e.g., face-to-face, telephone, digital technologies, group or individual support, proactive or reactive), the intensity of support (e.g., number of postnatal contacts), the person delivering the intervention (e.g., healthcare professional or layperson), and whether the effectiveness of support varied between high-income countries (HICs) and lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared additional breastfeeding support for healthy mothers of healthy term infants with standard maternity care. Support could be delivered face-to-face, via telephone, or through digital technologies. All included studies met established trustworthiness criteria. Data collection and analysis followed standard Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth methods, with two independent reviewers selecting trials, extracting data, and assessing the risk of bias and the trustworthiness of the studies. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. This updated review analyzed data from 116 trials, with 103 trials contributing data to the analyses, encompassing over 98,816 mother-infant pairs. Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that breastfeeding only support likely reduced the number of women discontinuing breastfeeding across all primary outcomes. Specifically, it reduced the risk of stopping any breastfeeding at six months (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.93, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.89 to 0.97), stopping exclusive breastfeeding at six months (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.93), stopping any breastfeeding at 4-6 weeks (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.97), and stopping exclusive breastfeeding at 4-6 weeks (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.90). Similar trends were observed for secondary breastfeeding outcomes, except for any breastfeeding at two months and 12 months, where the evidence was uncertain regarding the effectiveness of breastfeeding only support. The evidence for breastfeeding plus interventions was less consistent. For primary outcomes, moderate-certainty evidence indicated that breastfeeding plus support likely reduced the number of women stopping any breastfeeding (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.97) and exclusive breastfeeding at six months (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.90). However, the evidence was very uncertain regarding its effect on reducing the number of women stopping exclusive breastfeeding at 4-6 weeks (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95). Additionally, breastfeeding plus support likely had little to no effect on the number of women stopping any breastfeeding at 4-6 weeks (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.08). For secondary outcomes, it was unclear whether breastfeeding plus support reduced the number of women stopping any or exclusive breastfeeding at any time points. There were no consistent findings regarding non-breastfeeding outcomes, such as maternal satisfaction with care or feeding method, infant morbidity, and maternal mental health, except for a potential reduction in diarrhea among infants in the intervention groups. The overall risk of bias in the included trials was mixed. Blinding of participants and personnel was not feasible for these types of interventions, and the reliance on self-reported breastfeeding data introduced a potential risk of bias in outcome assessment. Meta-regression analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity in the primary outcomes, considering factors such as the person providing care, mode of delivery, intensity of support, and the income status of the country. The findings suggested that moderate levels of breastfeeding only support (defined as 4-8 visits) might be associated with greater benefits for exclusive breastfeeding at 4-6 weeks and six months. Additionally, breastfeeding only support appeared to be more effective in reducing the number of women in LMICs discontinuing exclusive breastfeeding at six months compared to women in HICs. However, no other differential effects were identified, and substantial heterogeneity remained unexplained. The meta-regression also indicated no significant differences in effectiveness based on the person providing support or the mode of delivery, although the statistical power was limited. In conclusion, offering breastfeeding only support to women likely increases the duration and exclusivity of breastfeeding, particularly in the first three to four months postpartum. The evidence for breastfeeding plus interventions is less certain. Support can be provided by healthcare professionals, laypersons, or a combination of both, and it can be delivered face-to-face, via telephone, or through digital technologies. A schedule of four to eight visits may enhance the effectiveness of these interventions. Further research is needed to identify the key components of effective interventions and to implement them on a larger scale.
